segments.text: My history.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I was originally a carpenter and a farmhand in the Central Coast of California and decided that I wanted to go back to school and did two years of computer science and then decided that I didn't want to spend the rest of my life
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: looking at a computer monitor in a basement, bad decision, and decided that I wanted to try to become an MD, which was a hard thing to try to do in the late 70s.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So that was a real stretch objective.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Went to UC Davis after two years of undergrad at San Barbara City College.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: and wanted to work on this new tech space called molecular biology.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And in particular on cancer, my mother was deathly afraid of breast cancer.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And so I looked around and found a laboratory at UC Davis with a guy named Bob Cardiff and another guy named Murray Gardner that were working with retroviruses and their links to breast cancer.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And it just happened that while I was in there, this is circa 83, 84, this whole thing cut loose in San Francisco with the Immunodeficiency Syndrome in men.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And the lab ended up right at the forefront of that.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: You know, Davis is just down the street basically from San Francisco.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And at the Davis Primate Center, they had discovered that there were monkeys that had immunodeficiency.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And so I was there in the lab as an undergraduate, as a total bench rat, when Preston Marks and Murray Gardner and others made the first discovery of a retrovirus basis for immunodeficiency in primates.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And then Murray went to the pastor.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: brought back the virus literally in his pocket.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: He went there with Bob Gallo, met with a guy named Luke Montagnier that you may know.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And that kind of kicked off the whole vaccine effort for AIDS.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So that's kind of what I cut my teeth on.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And so I came out of that.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: It was really bold to think that I could get into medical school.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I kind of overshot the mark.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I got an MD-PhD scholarship at Northwestern University in Chicago.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And so I went from having grown up in Santa Barbara with my wife, we were high school sweethearts, to Chicago.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And that was kind of an abrupt transition.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So we decided I would do my graduate work at San Diego.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I'd been accepted into a program
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: at UC San Diego that had two of the top gene therapy specialists.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I really wanted to do gene therapy with retroviruses.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: That was what I thought was going to be my life.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And so we moved down to San Diego and I started working in the laboratory of Inder Verma, which is in the Molecular Biology and Virology Labs at the Salk Institute.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And this is a place where graduate students normally aren't allowed to go.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: It was
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: There was seven Nobel laureates at the time, plus Jonas, a really intense competitive environment.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Carved out a little niche that I was going to work on for my graduate work, which was asking questions about how retrovirus RNA is packaged.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And from that,
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I had to develop a series of technologies to manufacture RNA and structure it and eventually put it into cells.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And that, through a cascade of events, being at the right place at the right time, asking the right questions, surrounded by geniuses, led to this series of discoveries that now forms the basis of the RNA technology platform that gives rise to these vaccines.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
